1Boundary points and closed sets

The lecture recalls the one-variable Extreme Value Theorem, then builds the vocabulary needed to state it for two variables. First: boundary point and closed set.

Top left of the board there is a short underlined heading that starts “14.7” (the rest is too faint to read), and under it a one-variable reminder: the graph of with the interval from to marked in red on the -axis.

Theorem (one variable)

EVT: continuous on , then attains absolute max. and min. values on .

Definition

Let be a set of points in . A boundary point of is a point around which every disc of positive radius contains both points in and points not in .

In the second photo “positive” is underlined as well.

Under the definition, a sketch: a set in the plane (labelled ), with a few points marked and a small disc drawn around each.

Explanation (added)

The test is about what is near the point, not about whether the point itself belongs to . So a boundary point may or may not be in . “Every disc” matters: a point deep inside also has some huge disc that reaches outside , but it has a small disc that does not, so it fails the test.

Definition

is closed if it contains all of its boundary points.

Examples

is closed.

is not closed.

Each has a small sketch beside it: a filled disc with a solid edge for the first, a hatched disc with a dashed edge for the second.

Board sketches, redrawn to scale (ticks every 1 unit). Solid edge: the circle belongs to the set. Dashed edge: it does not.

Explanation (added)

Both sets have the same boundary points: the circle of radius 3. With the circle is part of the set, so the set contains all of its boundary points and is closed. With the whole circle is left out, so it is not closed. This is the two-variable version of (endpoints included) against (endpoints left out).

2Bounded sets

The second property the theorem needs. A set can be closed without being bounded, and bounded without being closed.

Definition

is bounded if it is contained within some disc of finite radius.

Below the definition, a set that fails this: the curve , a vertical line labelled , and the region between the curve and the -axis to the right of that line, hatched. In the later photo a large circle has been drawn over the picture, and an arrow points at the hatched region with the words “not bounded.”

The label under the vertical line is small; it reads . The typed diagram below starts its region at 1 instead. Either way the region is unbounded.

Explanation (added)

The region is . It contains the point for every , and those points get as far from the origin as you like, so no disc of finite radius holds all of them. With its edges included this region is closed, so it is an example of closed but not bounded. The open disc from Section 1 is the opposite: bounded (it sits inside the disc of radius 3) but not closed.

3The Extreme Value Theorem for two variables

With “closed” and “bounded” defined, the theorem can be stated. Then the three steps for finding the absolute max and min.

Theorem

The Extreme Value Theorem (for functions of Two Variables). If is continuous on a closed, bounded set in , then attains an absolute max. and an absolute min. at some points in the region.

Explanation (added)

This is Stewart §14.7, Theorem 8. Compare it with the one-variable theorem in Section 1: is a closed, bounded interval, and “closed, bounded set” is what replaces it. Both words are needed. On the open disc (not closed), gets as close to 3 as you like but never equals 3, so it has no absolute max. On the region of Section 2 (not bounded), grows without limit. The theorem says the max and min exist; it does not say where they are. That is the job of the three steps below.

To the right of the theorem, a sketch labelled : a piece of surface floating above a region of the -plane, drawn on 3-D axes, with written underneath (the exponent is small).

Lower on the same board, a second sketch: a dome with level rings drawn around it, standing over a small four-sided region of the -plane with a dot in it.

To find abs. max./mins:

  1. Find critical points.
  2. Find extreme values on boundary.
  3. See max./mins.
Explanation (added)

These are Stewart’s three steps for a continuous on a closed, bounded set (§14.7, box 9): find the values of at the critical points inside ; find the extreme values of on the boundary of ; then the largest of all those values is the absolute max and the smallest is the absolute min. Step 3 on the board (“See max./mins.”) is that comparison.

Why it works: the theorem says an absolute max exists. If it is at a point inside , it is also a local max, so by the theorem from Nov 6 it is a critical point (, or a partial derivative does not exist). Otherwise it is on the boundary. The same goes for the min. It is the Closed Interval Method from Calc I (Stewart §4.1) with “endpoints” replaced by “boundary”. The Second Derivatives Test is not needed here, because the values are simply compared.

Explanation (added)

Only points on the red curve are allowed. Walk along it and watch which level curve of you are standing on. Wherever the red curve crosses a level curve, one side of the crossing is on higher level curves and the other side on lower ones, so is still changing and you are not at a max. At the point with the largest , the red curve cannot cross: it has to stay on one side of that level curve, which means the two curves touch and share a tangent line. In the board’s picture, never meets the red curve, crosses it, and is the largest level that still reaches it. This is the picture in Stewart §14.8, Figure 1.

10Parallel gradients and the method

A common tangent turns into an equation between gradients. The same reasoning works with three variables, and it gives a list of equations to solve.

So their normal lines are identical, so and have parallel gradient vectors:

for some real number .

Explanation (added)

From §14.6: is perpendicular to the level curve of through , and is perpendicular to the level curve . If the two curves have the same tangent line at the point, both gradients are perpendicular to that one line, so they point along the same normal line. Two vectors along the same line are scalar multiples of each other, and is the scalar. (This needs .) can be positive or negative: the gradients may point the same way or opposite ways.

Similarly, to find extreme values of subject to constraint , we want to find a point on the level surface for which has large/small as possible.

If is max. then the level surface

should be tangent to the level surface , so their gradient vectors should be parallel:

for some .

After “evaluate at all such points”, Stewart finishes: the largest of those values is the maximum of on the constraint and the smallest is the minimum, provided those extreme values exist (and on ). is a helper: it usually has to be eliminated to solve the system, but its value is not part of the answer.

What a typical exam question looks like
  1. Absolute max and min on a closed, bounded region. Given a polynomial and a rectangle (or a triangle or a disc), find the absolute maximum and minimum values. Find the critical points inside, turn each piece of the boundary into a one-variable problem, and compare all the values (Sections 3 to 7).
  2. Closed and bounded. Decide whether a given set is closed, whether it is bounded, and whether the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees a max and min on it (Sections 1 to 3).
  3. Lagrange multipliers with two variables. Find the extreme values of subject to : write , , , solve, and evaluate at each solution (Section 11).
  4. An applied problem with a constraint. A can or a box with a fixed surface area: name the variables, write the quantity to maximize as and the constraint as , then use Lagrange multipliers (Section 8).
  5. Explain the method. Say why, at a constrained maximum, the level curve of is tangent to , and why that gives (Sections 9 and 10).

Tests are written without a calculator, so answers stay exact, like , or .
